newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - PNG seeks stability, and share market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - PNG seeks stability, and share market.

text.p: A risky place to live at the best of times, the South Pacific nation of Papua New Guinea hopes to convince investors and companies that it is nevertheless a safe place to do business.
The PNG parliament will vote in late March on legislation to govern a local stock exchange that will attract home-grown firms and multinational giants, if all goes according to plan.
Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan, keen on another term in office after elections to be held in May or June this year, wants the share market up and running in time for the poll.
Chan is likely to campaign on a platform of sound economic management and the government's ability to attract foreign investment to a Third World nation with an average annual income of only US$700.

International investors, whose money will be central to the success of a PNG share market, will closely watch political developments following the government's controversial decision to use African mercenaries on the PNG island of Bougainville.

The island's giant Panguna copper mine, owned by Anglo-Australian miner RTZ-CRA, was sabotaged and closed by a secessionist uprising in May 1989 that the government has been unable to control, causing it long-term political embarrassment.

"If it (using mercenaries) were to solve the Bougainville problem it would probably be favourable to investment," a senior government source told Reuters, speaking anonymously. "But the way the story has been run at the moment, it is probably negative in the short term."
In fact, various PNG governments have spoken for the past 10 years about the attraction of a local share market.

But PNG's ability to attract stable foreign investment has been hurt by tribal and gang violence that led to a "shoot to kill" night curfew still in operation, landowner disputes that have disrupted major mine sites, and economic policy gaffes. BROKERS HAVE TO BE CONVINCED

At least three brokerage firms will be sought to provide a conduit for investors and to help attract liquidity. The only firms in town -- Merrill Lynch and the Malaysian-owned Kina Securities -- are solid candidates.
Melbourne-based McIntosh Securities, taken over by Merrill Lynch last month, has been active in PNG for more than 10 years.

McIntosh and Kina were involved in the A$261 million (US$202.54 million) float of the government's Orogen minerals arm late last year that was heavily sought by international institutions and PNG funds and residents.

Orogen Minerals Ltd, and Lihir Gold Ltd, both listed on the Australian Stock Exchange, are cited as two definite inaugural listings on a PNG exchange, along with Niugini Mining Ltd and Oil Search Ltd.

Peter Marshman, an adviser to the share market project, said other companies that might be lured are The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, Westpac Banking Corp and Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. Each blue-chip firm has sizeable and long-term operations in PNG.
Marshman, a retired former executive with the Australian Stock Exchange, admits the mid-year timetable is tight.

"We have a chicken-and-egg situation here. We don't think we are going to find it easy to attract brokers or listed companies until we have the infrastructure in place," he said, adding that the PNG central bank was providing some seed money.
Spokesmen for BHP and another large miner with interests in PNG, RTZ-CRA, said any listing proposal would be considered, but it would not be a priority. LINK TO WORLD BANK TALKS NEXT MONTH
The Washington-based World Bank, a sometimes critic of PNG policies, supports the stock exchange proposal and is likely to provide technical and financial assistance.
Negotiations between the PNG government and the World Bank begin next month for a new US$50 million loan that will hinge on the nation's commitment to financial sector reform.
The government's support for a stock exchange should be favourably received by the Washington bureaucrats, said one source involved in the negotiations.

A preliminary meeting was held in Washington earlier this month, with both sides on much friendlier terms than last year when Chan called the World Bank's demand for economic reform a "straitjacket policy".
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
